review_policy: Source inspected by assistant; not independent human/instructor approval; none is enabled in live explanation or Cambridge rule registries.

scope.precondition: An unmarked two-daughter S contains the subject NP and predicate VP; do not generalize to every clause configuration.

pedagogy.short: A clause displayed with an S node may be divided into a subject NP and predicate VP.
pedagogy.expanded: Explain each daughter's role only when the actual B–R construction is S → NP VP; another NP inside VP does not become a second subject.

positive.explanation: The children forms subject NP; laugh forms predicate VP.

contrast.explanation: The boy can be an object NP inside VP, not a second subject.

scope.precondition: Selected phrase category and its grammatical function are separately established.

pedagogy.short: NP is a category; subject is a possible function of an NP.
pedagogy.expanded: Determine functions using licensed parent/sister relations, not the NP label in isolation. A phrase may have different functions in different sentences.

positive.explanation: She and him are both NPs in the B–R analysis, but they perform different functions.

scope.precondition: In a licensed S → NP VP configuration, the NP immediately dominated by S is the subject.

pedagogy.short: An NP immediately dominated by an ordinary S is its subject.
pedagogy.expanded: Require immediate S dominance and a sister VP, not just a pronoun, word order, or a distant NP ancestor.

positive.explanation: I is the subject NP when immediately dominated by S.

contrast.explanation: You belongs to an NP under VP and is not S's subject NP.

scope.precondition: In a licensed S → NP VP configuration, the VP immediately dominated by S is the predicate.

pedagogy.short: The VP that is a direct daughter of the clause's S functions as its predicate.
pedagogy.expanded: A VP nested within another VP, as in auxiliary constructions, cannot automatically be called the top-level predicate.

positive.explanation: The predicate of the basic S spans hate you.

scope.precondition: The head is the essential center of a phrase; modifiers are dependent on that head.

pedagogy.short: The phrase's head fixes its grammatical type in the B–R explanation.
pedagogy.expanded: Optional modifiers depend on the head; do not call an element a head without a licensed tree analysis. Do not confuse a modifier with a selected complement.

positive.explanation: Birds can head the subject NP, while unusual supplies modification.

scope.precondition: Ordinary B–R NP contains a noun head, possibly with modifiers; exceptions include pronouns, names and coordination.

pedagogy.short: A noun may determine which NP the full expression is about.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not automatically assume the last noun is the head; an embedded noun may belong to an internal phrase.

positive.sentence: The actor in the garden laughed.
positive.explanation: Actor, not garden, is the head of the subject NP.

scope.precondition: A standalone pronoun functions as a complete NP in the third-edition B–R representation.

pedagogy.short: A pronoun such as she may fill a whole NP without a determiner.
pedagogy.expanded: Keep the pronoun's lexical category distinct from the full NP category; actual subject/object function depends on the surrounding tree.

positive.explanation: She can realize a one-word subject NP.

contrast.explanation: Her may realize a one-word object NP.

scope.precondition: A standalone proper name can be a complete non-branching NP under B–R's chapter conventions.

pedagogy.short: A proper name can fill the syntactic position of a full NP.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not invent an empty determiner as the normal representation of a bare name.

positive.explanation: Alex can realize a complete subject NP.

scope.precondition: Coordinate names or NPs may form a single NP with multiple coordinated heads.

pedagogy.short: A coordinated NP is one larger phrase, not necessarily two separate subjects.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not split a coordinate subject into separate subjects based solely on the presence of and.

positive.explanation: Alex and Robin together can form one subject NP.

scope.precondition: Book's introductory coordination criterion tests the compatibility of constituent categories.
exceptions: CGEL Ch. 2 p. 45 explicitly discusses coordination across unlike categories.

pedagogy.short: Burton-Roberts uses same-category coordination as a key phrase test in this chapter.
pedagogy.expanded: This is an analysis within the B–R instructional framework; Cambridge treats some unlike-category coordinations differently. Do not turn this introductory principle into a universal error detector.

positive.sentence: In the garden and under the tree, flowers grew.
positive.explanation: Two PPs can be coordinated in an English adjunct.

scope.precondition: Lexical verbs differ in which complements their particular sense licenses.

pedagogy.short: Verb complementation depends on the verb and its construction, not just the presence of a following phrase.
pedagogy.expanded: A verb may have more than one valency frame or meaning; do not diagnose a missing object from a generic V label alone.

positive.explanation: Play can be used without an NP object.
Play can also be used with an object NP.

scope.precondition: In the B–R transitive VP construction a V marked [trans] has a sister NP complement.

pedagogy.short: An NP that is sister to a transitive V may function as its direct object.
pedagogy.expanded: Require the reviewed [trans] feature and a compatible VP daughter relation; don't equate any adjacent NP with an object.

positive.explanation: You is the direct-object NP when sister to a licensed transitive head.

contrast.explanation: You is subject in the second sentence, not object.

scope.precondition: Feature [trans] denotes the transitive lexical-verb subcategory in B–R phrase markers.

pedagogy.short: The B–R [trans] feature records that a direct-object NP is selected in this VP.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not transfer this feature to every instance of the verb regardless of sense, or claim grammatical correctness from the presence of the feature.

positive.explanation: The transitive reading includes the object NP the painting.

scope.precondition: B–R intransitive lexical V requires no complement as sister in the basic VP.

pedagogy.short: An intransitive V can itself constitute a complete lexical VP.
pedagogy.expanded: An optional following PP need not be a selected complement; check actual construction and special lexical uses.

positive.explanation: A complete VP can be formed without a direct-object NP.

scope.precondition: B–R double-object ditransitives select two NP complements with distinct roles.

pedagogy.short: In a licensed two-NP VP, the first complement commonly acts as indirect object and the second as direct object.
pedagogy.expanded: Only apply in a reviewed ditransitive configuration, not to every pair of NPs; other ditransitive realizations with PP should remain distinguishable.

positive.explanation: Him and a book have different complement roles in this construction.

scope.precondition: A PP may be an optional modifier rather than a required verb complement in certain B–R constructions.

pedagogy.short: A PP following a verb is not automatically its complement.
pedagogy.expanded: Some verbs select PPs as complements in other constructions; keep this principle conditional on valency evidence.

positive.explanation: In the garden can be an optional location modifier.

contrast.explanation: On her friend is more closely selected by the verb and should not be called optional adjunct by surface order.

scope.precondition: B–R basic branching NP has DET and NOM as sister daughters; pronoun and name NPs are special nonbranching cases.

pedagogy.short: DET and NOM jointly form an ordinary branching NP in the B–R model.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not force pronouns and names into DET + NOM; don't omit possible empty-DET analysis for plural/mass noun NPs.

positive.explanation: The determiner the is distinct from the nominal students.

contrast.explanation: The pronoun they realizes NP without the basic branching DET–NOM pattern.

scope.precondition: B–R NOM is the level between NP and N that includes head-noun modifiers.

pedagogy.short: NOM groups a noun with any supported modifications below NP.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not identify arbitrary PP/relative attachments as NOM modifiers without source-approved structure.

positive.explanation: Red modifies car in the nominal constituent.

scope.precondition: B–R permits an empty DET in certain indefinite/general plural count and mass-noun NPs.

pedagogy.short: An unpronounced determiner slot is not a missing word error by itself.
pedagogy.expanded: The source limits this to licensed noun types; proper names/pronouns have distinct representations and are not governed by this empty-DET analysis.

positive.explanation: A plural noun can head an NP with an unpronounced DET in the B–R analysis.
A mass noun can likewise occur in the licensed pattern.

contrast.explanation: A singular count NP with pronounced article is a different case.

scope.precondition: Distinguish lexical have (with NP complement) from perfect auxiliary have (taking a VP complement).

pedagogy.short: The same spelling had may serve different grammatical constructions.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not blame had or impose perfect-participle requirements until its lexical/auxiliary status and selected complement are supported.

positive.explanation: Had is used as a lexical verb with NP complement.
Had is perfect auxiliary with a verbal complement.

scope.precondition: Perfect auxiliary have selects what Burton-Roberts calls a perfect-participle verbal form.
exceptions: Ellipsis may leave the verbal complement unpronounced in an appropriate discourse context.

pedagogy.short: Within a confirmed perfect construction the following verb has the nonfinite perfect-participle form.
pedagogy.expanded: Different verbs have identical or distinct preterite/participle spellings; source rule is not a live detector and exceptions/ellipsis must be handled.

positive.explanation: Gone follows the perfect auxiliary.
Wanted has the same surface form as its preterite but a different constructional role.

contrast.explanation: Went is preterite; this candidate illustrates a form-selection mismatch pending verified diagnosis.

scope.precondition: Progressive be selects what Burton-Roberts calls the progressive-participle -ing form.

pedagogy.short: Progressive auxiliary be is followed by an -ing verbal form in the normal licensed construction.
pedagogy.expanded: Lexical copular be followed by an adjective is a different construction; don't infer PROG from be spelling alone.

positive.explanation: Reading follows a progressive auxiliary.
Is can be a lexical copula instead.

scope.precondition: B–R auxiliary heads VP with a VP complement; nested VP hierarchy is not synonymous with VP adjunct modification.

pedagogy.short: An auxiliary heads an outer VP and selects an inner VP.
pedagogy.expanded: Keep the actual licensed auxiliary sequence and phrase-marker structure rather than replacing it with Cambridge's clause model.

positive.explanation: Multiple auxiliary heads can form nested VPs.
The perfect auxiliary heads a VP containing a complement VP.

scope.precondition: After a modal auxiliary the following lexical/auxiliary verb takes a nonfinite stem form in B–R's description.

pedagogy.short: A modal selects a verb stem form in its VP complement.
pedagogy.expanded: Check genuine modal status and syntactic construction before using this as an error claim; do not apply to modal meaning alone.

positive.explanation: Swim is the stem following modal can.

contrast.explanation: A candidate mismatch; not a live correction verdict.

scope.precondition: CGEL distinguishes a sentence as a text-level syntactic unit from a clause as a subject–predicate construction; B–R S is a separate formal convention.

pedagogy.short: Cambridge uses the concept of a clause for the relevant subject–predicate structure, not an S node identical to B–R S.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not relabel the canonical B–R phrase marker as a Cambridge clause node: its ontology differs in part.

positive.explanation: This entire utterance can be a sentence and has clause structure.
She smiled is an embedded clause, not an independent sentence here.

scope.precondition: CGEL canonical vs noncanonical distinguishes basic structure from negatives, questions, passives and subordinate clauses.

pedagogy.short: A noncanonical clause construction is not automatically ungrammatical.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not flag ordinary questions, passives or negation just because they differ from S → NP VP word order.

positive.explanation: Subject–auxiliary inversion is a noncanonical interrogative construction.
Passive is noncanonical in CGEL's organizational contrast, not incorrect.

scope.precondition: Core modal auxiliaries lack many nonfinite inflections and do not take third-person -s agreement in the ordinary sense.

pedagogy.short: Modal status constrains which inflected forms a modal can have.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not equate every verb expressing possibility with the core modal inflectional paradigm.

positive.explanation: Can does not become cans for third-person singular subject.

scope.precondition: One written word form can realize more than one inflectional category in different constructions.

pedagogy.short: An identical spelling does not prove a verb has the same form category in every sentence.
pedagogy.expanded: Use the governing verb-form selection environment to distinguish preterite from past participle in syncretic cases.

positive.explanation: Wanted is preterite here.
Wanted is a past participle here.

scope.precondition: CGEL describes ordering restrictions among modal, perfect, progressive and passive auxiliaries.

pedagogy.short: An auxiliary sequence is constrained in order, not arbitrary.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not translate CGEL structural categories directly into B–R labels; special uses, ellipsis and coordination require separate checks.

positive.explanation: This follows the modal→perfect→passive selection order.

scope.precondition: CGEL separates modal→plain, perfect→past participle, progressive→gerund-participle and passive→past participle.
exceptions: Separate lexical uses of have/be; syncretism and irregular verb paradigms; auxiliary ellipsis.

pedagogy.short: Each eligible auxiliary constrains the form of the following verb.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not infer that auxiliary spelling alone determines structure; identify perfect/progressive/passive construction, syncretism and special cases.

positive.explanation: Modal selects plain leave.
Perfect selects past participle left.
Progressive selects -ing leaving.

contrast.explanation: Illustrative potential violation: went is the preterite of go.

scope.precondition: Present perfect normally does not combine with adjuncts that put the event wholly in a completed past period, but CGEL describes contextual exceptions.
exceptions: Restricted experiential perfect contexts and varieties/discourse interpretation must be evaluated.

pedagogy.short: Whether a past-time adjunct is compatible with a present-perfect clause depends on the interpretation.
pedagogy.expanded: Never implement a blanket present-perfect plus yesterday blacklist. Experiential perfect and discourse context can affect acceptability.

positive.explanation: Simple preterite allows a definite past-time reference.

exception.explanation: CGEL explicitly discusses restricted experiential readings of a similar construction.

scope.precondition: CGEL distinguishes transitivity from valency (number of complements) and recognizes that PP complements may be non-core.

pedagogy.short: Verb subcategory cannot be inferred only from the count of following NPs.
pedagogy.expanded: The same verb may license several different complementation patterns; don't use CGEL valency as a direct alias for all B–R V features.

positive.explanation: A ditransitive clause has distinct object complements.
A PP can be a selected complement rather than an optional adjunct.

scope.precondition: Verb selection licenses complements; adjuncts are not subject to the same lexeme-specific licensing test.

pedagogy.short: An NP or PP is not classified as complement solely because it follows a verb.
pedagogy.expanded: Verify actual lexical sense, preposition and construction. Not all complements are obligatory.

positive.explanation: The verb licenses an NP object in this reading.
Yesterday can be an adjunct without a selected head verb.

scope.precondition: Some prepositional complements require the particular preposition selected by their governing verb.

pedagogy.short: The identity of a preposition can be part of a verb's complementation pattern.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not turn all different prepositions into errors; meaning shifts and optional adjuncts must be distinguished.

positive.explanation: On is selected by depend in this construction.

contrast.explanation: At is selected in this particular sense, unlike looked for the painting.

scope.precondition: Verbs can license particular subordinate clause types as their complements.

pedagogy.short: A subordinate clause's role depends on the governing verb and the licensed clause construction.
pedagogy.expanded: Do not classify every subordinate clause as object or adjunct without checking the relevant verb and clause type.

positive.sentence: She wondered whether he was ready.
positive.explanation: The interrogative clause can complement wonder.

positive.sentence: She knew that he was ready.
positive.explanation: The declarative clause can complement know.

scope.precondition: CGEL distinguishes obligatory and optional complements; absence does not always imply missing arguments.

pedagogy.short: A complement can sometimes be omitted without making the clause unacceptable.
pedagogy.expanded: A selected relation differs from obligatory occurrence; review verb sense and context, not merely transitivity labels.

positive.explanation: Book NP is a complement in the transitive reading.
Read can appear without an overt object in another licensed reading.

crosswalks.issue: B–R S phrase-marker label vs CGEL clause category; CGEL reserves sentence for text-unit analysis.
B–R Ch.3 introduces same-category coordination as a test, whereas CGEL Ch.2 p.45 allows unlike-category coordination. Context-specific analysis needed.
The books partly overlap on selection while classifying valency, optional complements and non-core PP differently; do not equate every label or require every complement overt.
B–R perfect participle corresponds to CGEL past participle in reviewed perfect-have selection, but categories are not all identical.
B–R progressive participle vs CGEL gerund-participle in reviewed progressive-be selection.
B–R nonfinite stem form and CGEL plain form terminology for modal-selected verb; source scopes differ.
Form-selection similarities do not prove equivalent constituent tree hierarchy; retain B–R nested VPs.
B–R auxiliary form selection alone does not license Cambridge's complete aspectual-adjunct semantics or contextual exceptions.

template_candidates.text: In {sentence}, {child_np_span} is the subject NP and {child_vp_span} is the predicate VP of the displayed S.
template_candidates.deep_text: This applies only to the approved B–R S → NP VP construction; another sentence type may require a different structure.

template_candidates.text: The NP {target_surface} functions as the subject of the predicate {sister_surface}.
template_candidates.deep_text: This classification depends on immediate S dominance and a VP sister, not the NP label alone.

template_candidates.text: The VP {target_surface} functions as the predicate associated with subject {sister_surface}.
template_candidates.deep_text: An embedded VP in an auxiliary chain would require a different role explanation.

template_candidates.text: The pronoun {target_surface} realizes an NP; its sentence role depends on that NP's position.
template_candidates.deep_text: Do not call a pronoun a subject or object without a source-licensed parent relation.

template_candidates.text: The proper name {target_surface} can realize an NP in this structure.
template_candidates.deep_text: A name NP need not have an invented determiner.

template_candidates.text: The noun {target_surface} is the head of the NP {parent_np_span} in this analyzed construction.
template_candidates.deep_text: The head relation must be established from licensed structure, not by choosing the last noun.

template_candidates.text: The transitive verb {target_surface} takes the NP {selected_np_span} as direct-object complement.
template_candidates.deep_text: Only allowed when the [trans] construction and exact sister relationship are source-supported.

template_candidates.text: The NP {target_surface} functions as direct object of {governing_verb} in this licensed VP.
template_candidates.deep_text: The same category NP can instead be a subject in another position.

template_candidates.text: The NP {target_surface} occupies the {complement_position} position with {governing_verb}.
template_candidates.deep_text: The two object slots must be linked to an independently established ditransitive construction.

template_candidates.text: The VP {target_surface} is complete around its intransitive head {lexical_head} in this construction.
template_candidates.deep_text: A PP may still modify it; lack of overt object does not automatically prove intransitivity for arbitrary verbs.

template_candidates.text: In the NP {target_surface}, DET {det_span} combines with NOM {nom_span}.
template_candidates.deep_text: Pronoun and name NPs use different B–R representations.

template_candidates.text: The NOM {target_surface} contains head noun {head_noun} and supported modification {modifier_span}.
template_candidates.deep_text: Not every modifier may be asserted without a reviewed attachment.

template_candidates.text: This NP uses an unpronounced DET slot in a licensed {noun_number_or_mass} construction.
template_candidates.deep_text: An empty DET is not by itself an omission error.

template_candidates.text: The auxiliary {aux_surface} heads the displayed VP and selects the VP {inner_vp_span}.
template_candidates.deep_text: Form licensing is a separate grammatical constraint; do not infer a correction from the shape alone.

template_candidates.text: The form {target_surface} belongs to the {licensed_auxiliary_type} construction with a {complement_category} complement.
template_candidates.deep_text: Distinguish had breakfast from had eaten by complement structure before applying any participle claim.

template_candidates.text: The PP {target_surface} modifies VP {governing_vp_span} in the licensed analysis.
template_candidates.deep_text: Do not assume that every PP is an adjunct; some are lexically selected complements.
